newsitem.title: UK: Scientists say Britain concealed mad cow data.
newsitem.headline: Scientists say Britain concealed mad cow data.

text.p: Independent scientists accused the British government on Thursday of deliberately concealing data about mad cow disease and hampering research into the ailment which has devastated Europe's beef markets.

The scientists told the journal Nature the reluctance of the Ministry of Farming and Agriculture (MAFF) to provide information about Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy resulted from secrecy and insufficient staff to analyse and distribute information.
"This has worked to the detriment of the understanding (of the disease) and dissemination of information in general," one scientist said.
The journal said not all scientists had difficulty obtaining information but those that did felt their research had suffered as a result.
"It has been a nightmare to get hold of comprehensive data," John Kent, a statistician at the University of Leeds said. "Not having the numbers more easily available has made life difficult."
Concern over mad cow disease escalated in March after Britain disclosed a probable link between BSE and its human equivalent Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease, a fatal brain wasting disease.

Britain agreed to an additional cull of cattle most at risk of the disease in exchange for a promise to lift a European Union ban on the export of British beef and byproducts. It also plans to kill all cattle over 30 months old.

But after a report in August suggesting that the disease would die out on its own by the year 2001 and following protests by British farmers the government decided that an extra cull, agreed at an EU summit in June to defuse the crisis, was unnecessary. Nature said MAFF held back vital data from Roy Anderson, a professor of zoology at the University of Oxford who was trying to estimate the numbers of infected cattle that may have entered the food chain undetected.
"It was pretty clear that MAFF were scared about the outcome (of the study)," another unnamed scientist told Nature.
He suggested the government feared Anderson's study would prove that many more sick animals had entered the food chain than was previously thought, which it did.
A ministry spokeswoman dismissed the secrecy allegations, saying that access to data is permitted within agreed collaborative projects.

She told Nature that researchers can obtain whatever data they need "as long as we deem it possible, and as long as the data doesn't infringe on the confidentiality of individual farms or the Data Protection Act."
